what: The twenty-four sacred sites (pīṭha, upapīṭha …) with their names (Oḍḍiyāna, Jālandhara, Kāmarūpa, Pullīramalaya/Pūrṇagiri, Devīkoṭa …) and their mapping onto the body.

evidence.detail: The Laghuśaṃvara's list of 24 sites shares many names with Śaiva/Śākta pīṭha lists (Kubjikāmata, Kaulajñānanirṇaya).
The Buddhist account: Heruka subdued Maheśvara (Bhairava) and his retinue at the 24 sites and took them over as his maṇḍala.
Śaiva priority argued by A. Sanderson; others see a shared regional sacred geography.

what: Passages, deity-names, cremation-ground idiom and yoginī-cult elements of the Buddhist Yoginī tantras (Laghuśaṃvara, Abhidhānottara) paralleling Śaiva Vidyāpīṭha scriptures (Picumata-Brahmayāmala, Yoginīsaṃcāra of the Jayadrathayāmala).

evidence.detail: Sanderson identifies verses of the Laghuśaṃvara redacted from Śaiva Vidyāpīṭha texts; the extent and direction are debated by other scholars.
The Buddhist tradition presents the parallels as Heruka's subjugation and conversion of the Śaiva deities.

notes: No Śaiva text was compared locally; recorded as a hypothesis only.

what: The Mahāvairocana and Tattvasaṃgraha, their maṇḍalas (Womb and Vajra), mantras and consecrations, carried to China by Śubhakarasiṃha, Vajrabodhi and Amoghavajra and thence to Japan (Kūkai).

evidence.detail: Chinese translations: T 848 (Mahāvairocana, 724) and Amoghavajra's Tattvasaṃgraha.
The Shingon patriarchal lineage runs from Mahāvairocana and Vajrasattva through Nāgārjuna(bodhi), Vajrabodhi and Amoghavajra.

what: The six-limbed yoga with prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra, dhyāna, dhāraṇā and samādhi (Maitrī Upaniṣad: + tarka; Buddhist: + anusmṛti) — shared names, different order, signs and goal.

evidence.detail: GST 18.138 names the six limbs; the Maitrī Upaniṣad's six-limbed yoga uses five of the same names.
Dependence either way or a common pool of yoga vocabulary.

what: The dohā genre and its themes — critique of ritual, caste, scripture and pilgrimage, the body as the holy place, the innate (sahaja), the true guru — continued in Nāth and Sant poetry (Kabīr).

evidence.detail: sahaja, the true guru (satguru / bla ma dam pa), critique of the six systems, bathing places and idols.
Transmission via the Nāth yogīs is commonly suggested; no direct citation.

what: The figure of the kalkin — the future king from Śambhala who destroys the barbarians at the end of an age — and the name Śambhala, reworked as the dynasty of kalkin kings of the Kālacakra.

evidence.detail: Purāṇic Kalki is born in Śambhala-grāma and destroys the mlecchas; the Kālacakra's kalkin Raudra Cakrin defeats the barbarians.
Purāṇic precedence by date; the Kālacakra reinterprets 'kalkin' as the holder of the vajra family.

what: The four gnoses of the Yogācāra (mirror-like, equality, discriminating, accomplishing), with the dharmadhātu gnosis added, as the five gnoses of the five buddha families.

evidence.detail: The same four names in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra and the tantric five-gnosis scheme.
